clue.text: Real men, disturbed at weight-loss attempt by wealthy actress

indicators.note: disturbed means thrown into disorder, so the letters of real men are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
a diet is an attempt to lose weight
rich means wealthy

explanation.surface: Macho men are upset that a rich film star is trying to slim down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' turns REAL MEN into MARLENE; then come DIET and RICH. Marlene Dietrich was the German-born Hollywood star of The Blue Angel.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlene Dietrich was a famous German-American film star and singer, so she is an example of an actress.

clue.text: British mother with appendix disease

parts.note: Mum is the British word for mother (Americans say Mom)
a postscript, PS, is an addition at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A British mum suffering from a burst appendix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appendix' points at the organ in the surface, but it means an addition tacked on, as a postscript is.
explanation.definitionFit: Mumps is a contagious viral illness causing swollen glands in the neck.

clue.text: Quick to recover from toxic Listerine

indicators.note: something toxic is poisoned and spoilt, so the letters of the mouthwash are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, a brand of mouthwash and the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone bounces back fast after a bad reaction to Listerine mouthwash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toxic' is the signal to rearrange the nine letters of LISTERINE; 'from' just links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A resilient person or thing springs back quickly after a setback, so it is quick to bounce back.

clue.text: Foreign anime contains kid-friendly puzzle

indicators.note: 'contains' says the rearranged letters hold the rating letter inside them
foreign means strange or out of place, so the letters of anime are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange
G is the US film rating for general audiences, suitable for children

explanation.surface: A Japanese cartoon from abroad includes a puzzle suitable for children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign' rearranges ANIME into ENIMA, and 'contains' puts G inside it. G is the American film rating meaning fit for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is something mysterious or baffling, so it is a puzzle or riddle.

clue.text: Urge, for instance, to leave children in back

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for instance
to go is to leave

indicators.note: what is in the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An urge to leave the kids in the back seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In back' sounds like the back seat of a car; it picks out the end of children.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg on is a phrasal verb for encouraging or pushing someone to act.

clue.text: One "Mad Libs" vein gets hidden

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: mad means crazy and disordered, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, part of the fodder
taken as written, part of the fodder

explanation.surface: A Mad Libs word game has a hidden streak running through it.
explanation.walkthrough: Mad Libs is a US fill-in-the-blanks word game, so 'Mad' reads as part of its name; here it is the signal to rearrange the two words that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something invisible cannot be seen, so it is effectively hidden from view.

clue.text: Toddler captivates girl in Swiss novel or Russian novel

indicators.note: to captivate is to hold captive, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a tot is a small child
Heidi is the girl in Johanna Spyri's Swiss children's novel

explanation.surface: A little child is charmed by Heidi, or by a Russian classic.
explanation.walkthrough: TOT opens to hold HEIDI: T + HEIDI + OT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Idiot is Dostoevsky's 1869 novel about the saintly Prince Myshkin.

clue.text: Exists to circumvent anti-narcotics bureau's plans

indicators.note: circumventing literally means going around, so one piece is wrapped around the other

parts.note: is means exists
the Drug Enforcement Administration is the US anti-drug agency

explanation.surface: Something exists to get around the drug agency's plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circumvent' reads as evade, but literally it means to go around.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideas are plans or proposals one has thought up.

clue.text: Greeting Fonteyn's upside-down chart

parts.note: hi is a greeting

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upside-down makes the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: Margot Fonteyn was the great British ballerina; with the possessive s

explanation.surface: Greeting a ballerina whose dance chart is the wrong way up.
explanation.walkthrough: The ballerina's first name, with the possessive s, is read backwards after HI.
explanation.definitionFit: A histogram is a bar chart showing how often values fall into ranges.

clue.text: Truant to deliver the wrong note?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read playfully: to sing a note wrongly, as a prefix plus a verb

explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer as MIS-SING, to sing amiss; the question mark flags that this sense is invented for the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant pupil is absent from class, which is to say not present where expected.

clue.text: TV audience competes to grab and return the rewind button

indicators.note: grabbing something holds it inside your grip, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to vie is to compete

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: REW is the label on a tape player's rewind button

explanation.surface: Television viewers fight over the remote to rewind a programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Tape players and VCRs label their buttons with short codes such as PLAY, FF and the one used here.
explanation.definitionFit: The people watching a television programme are collectively its viewers.

clue.text: Last bit of graham crackers outside the workplace

indicators.note: one word standing outside another wraps around it

parts.note: saltines are American soda crackers

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A snack-time line about graham crackers and the office.
explanation.walkthrough: Saltines are a US cracker; they go round the M. 'The salt mines' is jokey slang for one's job, as in 'back to the salt mines'.
explanation.definitionFit: Back to the salt mines is an idiom for returning to work, so the salt mines stand for the workplace.

clue.text: Reduced the price (half off) for a club

indicators.note: half off means half the word is taken away, so only its first five of ten letters stay

parts.note: to discount is to reduce the price, so the past tense gives discounted
the second half of discounted

explanation.surface: A shop marked its prices down, half off, for members of a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half off' sounds like the size of the reduction, but it cuts DISCOUNTED in half. A disco is a nightclub for dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A disco is a nightclub where people dance to recorded music, so it is a kind of club.

clue.text: General (Confederate military leader) in hit series

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for general, as in a film rating
Robert E. Lee commanded the Confederate army in the US Civil War

explanation.surface: A Civil War general features in a popular history series.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket makes 'General' and the Confederate leader look like one man; they are two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Glee was a successful American television show about a high-school singing club.

clue.text: $1,000, and another $1,000 to cover Sid Vicious's descendants

indicators.note: something vicious is savage and violent, so the letters are mangled into a new order
in a down entry, a piece that covers another sits on top of it

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand dollars
K stands for a thousand
the name rearranged

explanation.surface: Paying two thousand dollars for Sid Vicious's heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid Vicious was the Sex Pistols' bassist; his surname is lifted to be the signal acting on Sid.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandchildren are descendants two generations down from someone.

clue.text: Explorer (for example, sociologist Max) goes around front of battle lines

indicators.note: going around something encircles it, so one piece encloses the rest

parts.note: Max Weber was a German sociologist

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter
rows are lines

explanation.surface: A famous sociologist cast as an explorer heading to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explorer' suggests an adventurer, but it is Internet Explorer, Microsoft's old program.
explanation.definitionFit: Internet Explorer was Microsoft's program for viewing pages online, an example of a web browser.

clue.text: Vast, mysterious rune enthralls a pursuer of pleasure

parts.note: epic means vast or huge in scale

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the rearranged letters hold the a inside them
mysterious means puzzling and obscure, so the letters of rune are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A huge, cryptic rune captivates someone devoted to pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mysterious' rearranges the letters of rune, and 'enthralls' holds the A inside that jumble; vast in the sense of grand in scale supplies the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicurean is devoted to sensual enjoyment, especially fine food and drink, after the philosopher Epicurus.

clue.text: Second mate's weird, trendy ocean liner

indicators.note: weird means strange and twisted, so the letters of mate's are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
hip means trendy or fashionable

explanation.surface: A ship's second mate is strange and fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second mate' reads as a ship's officer, fitting the liner, but second gives S and 'weird' rearranges MATE'S into TEAMS; HIP for trendy ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: A steamship is a vessel driven by steam engines, and the great ocean liners of the past were steamships.

clue.text: Some singers' method of detection: sit most of the way up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top
going most of the way stops short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: sonar detects underwater objects by sound
to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: Choristers explain how to spot something: sit almost upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' reads as sitting upright, but in a down entry it reverses everything before it, the detection method included.
explanation.definitionFit: Sopranos are singers with the highest voice range, so they are some of the singers in a choir.

clue.text: Gave permission to hit our translation within the limits of the English alphabet

indicators.note: 'within' places the rearranged letters inside the alphabet's limits

parts.words: the limits of the English alphabet
parts.note: the alphabet runs from A to Z, and the English call the last letter zed, so A and ZED

indicators.note: a translation turns words into a new form, so the letters of hit our are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A request for a licence to translate a hit, staying within the alphabet's letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translation' rearranges HIT OUR, and 'within' sets it between the alphabet's limits A and Z, with 'English' asking for Z said the British way, ZED, not the American zee.
explanation.definitionFit: To authorize something is to sanction or approve it, which is giving permission for it.

clue.text: Two forms of the same verb: "smile"

parts.note: the infinitive of the verb
the first-person present of the same verb, to be

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson offering two forms of the verb smile.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb is not 'smile' at all: it is 'to be', whose forms BE and AM join up.
explanation.definitionFit: To beam is to give a broad, happy smile.

clue.text: L could be used to complete the word C?IME (a movie genre)

parts.words: L could be used to complete the word C?IME
parts.note: surface reading: a fill-in-the-letter puzzle where L turns the gap into a word meaning climate; setter's reading: the answer goes before the clue's first letter, so the full sentence lists three letters joined by 'or', each of which completes the word

explanation.surface: A word puzzle asking which letter fits the gap in a film genre's name.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the answer then the clue: H or R or L could be used to complete C?IME, giving chime, crime or clime. The answer itself is a film genre too.
explanation.definitionFit: Horror is the film category built on fear and the supernatural, alongside crime as a genre.

clue.text: Object of doctor capturing flightless bird

indicators.note: capturing something holds it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
the emu is a large flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: A vet treating an emu, the bird being the doctor's patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' reads as a noun, the thing aimed at; it is the verb meaning to protest.
explanation.definitionFit: To demur is to raise an objection or show reluctance, a verb sense of object.

clue.text: Drink in a shoe? That's a laugh

parts.note: a moc is short for moccasin, a soft shoe
ha is the sound of a laugh

explanation.surface: Drinking from a shoe: what a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink in a shoe' suggests a toast from a slipper; 'in' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocha is a coffee drink, often flavoured with chocolate.

clue.text: Unreliable info: 21 is like a policeman, say

indicators.note: something unreliable cannot be trusted to stay the same, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the answer to 21 Across

explanation.surface: Untrustworthy information comes up when someone objects like a cop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unreliable info' looks like the definition, hearsay; 'Unreliable' is only the signal, and the answer to 21 joins the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A police officer on the beat typically wears a uniform, hence 'say' marking the example.

clue.text: It's me, breaking down parts of a list

indicators.note: breaking down means falling apart, so the letters of it's me are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone admits it is they who are falling apart over the bits of a to-do list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking down' looks like emotional collapse, but it rearranges the letters of IT'S ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Items are the individual entries on a list, so they are its parts.

clue.text: Sees fruit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: goes out with someone romantically
second meaning: the sweet brown fruit of a palm

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sees' sounds like spotting, but it means is going out with, as in 'she's seeing someone'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for courting someone and a noun for the fruit of the date palm.

clue.text: "Holy smoke!" in dramatic scene

indicators.note: dramatic suggests a theatrical flourish, so the letters of scene are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at a theatrical moment on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holy smoke!' looks like an exclamation of surprise, but read literally it is the sacred smoke burned in religious rites; 'dramatic' rearranges scene into CENSE, after IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Incense is aromatic resin burned in churches and temples, so its smoke is literally holy smoke.

clue.text: Corn, in demand in a perceptible range

parts.note: ears are the cobs of a corn plant
a hot product is in demand

explanation.surface: Corn is in demand and close enough to notice.
explanation.walkthrough: The singular 'Corn' stands for the crop as a whole, so its plural ears are fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Earshot is the distance within which a sound can be heard, a range of perception by hearing.

clue.text: Looks around, smooths voyage with the flag

indicators.note: one piece placed around the others encloses them

parts.note: stares are fixed looks
to sand wood is to smooth it
plain synonym

explanation.surface: A sailor eyes the ensign while smoothing out a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer word splits after its fourth letter to take in the two inner pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stars and Stripes is the popular name of the flag of the United States.
